# Cybernaut-mini: scope decisions (2026-07-28)

Decisions agreed with the user before planning the cybernaut-mini rebuild.
Reference blog: https://nosible.com/blog/the-road-to-cybernaut-1
Local copies: `data/00_reference/the-road-to-cybernaut-1.md` and `.build-guide.md`.

## Goal
Reverse-engineer the NOSIBLE Cybernaut-1 retrieval stack as a *learning* repo.
Every component must carry direct blog references, stated assumptions, what the
code does to overcome them, and which alternatives were rejected and why.

## Locked decisions

1. **Layout — stage-numbered packages.** `build/` (Part A), `query/s1_language`
   … `query/s8_retrieve` (Part B stages 1-8), `agent/` (Part C), `core/`
   (rrf, models, config, trace). Splits the current `routing.py`, which today
   fuses blog stages 5 AND 6 into one function.

2. **Scope — all offline-capable NOT-BUILT components.** harmonic-TFIDF search
   intents with POS filtering, instruction-template system, bloom filters,
   trained zstd dictionaries, Aho-Corasick full-text intent pass, Bayesian dense
   selector, Personalized PageRank reranker, prompt-injection rules,
   multilingual stages 1-2. Neural reranker / LLM judge / LLM summaries stay
   pluggable providers.

3. **Corpus — REAL DATA ONLY. User was emphatic: "THIS MUST NEVER USE DUMMY
   DATA."** The existing 63-doc synthetic corpus and its fabricated judgments
   are to be removed.
   - Primary: BEIR SciFact (~5.2k real PubMed abstracts, real qrels,
     CC BY-SA 4.0 as `BeIR/scifact`; note original `allenai/scifact` is tagged
     CC BY-NC 2.0 — data needs its own attribution/licence file, not MIT).
   - Multilingual: MIRACL Japanese slice (Apache-2.0, ungated) so the blog's
     actual Japanese query exercises stages 1-2.
   - Test fixtures: a small slice of REAL docs + REAL qrels committed to
     `data/01_raw/`, licence permitting.

4. **Kedro — the 8-stage query pipeline becomes a REAL Kedro pipeline**, not a
   viz-only DAG. User reaffirmed this after being told the cost (per-query
   session overhead, awkward for the agent's dynamic re-invocation); their
   reason is educational value. Resolution: the 8 stages are real Kedro nodes
   runnable via `kedro run --pipeline query` and visible in `kedro viz`; the
   agent re-invokes those same nodes programmatically through `SequentialRunner`
   over an in-memory catalog, so there is no duplicate implementation and no
   disk round-trip.

5. **Embedder — hash embedder REMOVED.** Real embeddings only
   (`intfloat/multilingual-e5-small`, MIT, ungated). Consequence the user
   accepted: slower tests, model download, harder byte-determinism.
   Open recommendation not yet ruled on: `model2vec` static embeddings are
   real (distilled from a real model, not a hash) and ~500x faster — a way to
   keep tests fast without reintroducing a fake.

6. **Docs enforcement — executable checker.** `make docs-check` must FAIL when:
   a package dir lacks README.md, a README lacks a ```mermaid block, a module
   lacks its blog-reference/Assumptions/Alternatives docstring header, or a blog
   anchor is dead. Wired into a git pre-commit hook, `make check`, and CI.
   Prose in AGENTS.md alone was explicitly rejected as unenforceable.

7. **Learning formats — all four.** Folder READMEs with mermaid; a runnable

   `cybernaut-mini explain --stage N` CLI inspector.

8. **Commits — one per build-guide Part E milestone**, each independently green
   (tests + lint + types + docs-check).

# Nosible Hugging Face Artifacts: Models & Datasets

# Nosible Hugging Face Artifacts: Models & Datasets

> Digest of `docs/huggingface-archive/` (ingested 2026-07-29). Related: [[docs-archive-overview]], [[nosible-blog-archive-research-engineering-digest]], [[nosible-py-official-nosible-search-api-client]], [[smol-html-html-cleaner-minifier-for-web-scale-ingest]].

The one layer of the NOSIBLE stack needing **no reverse-engineering** — weights and 300k labelled rows are downloadable. Guide §3's output.

## Models (5 repos, all Apache-2.0)

All are 596M-param `qwen3` causal LMs fine-tuned from `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base`, run as **constrained single-token classifiers**. v1.1 released 2025-11-25 (served live by featherless-ai); v1.2 released 2026-04-28 (weights only). No `prediction-v1.2`.

| Model | Task | Labels | Downloads |
|---|---|---|---|
| `financial-sentiment-v1.2-base` | valence (financial impact) | positive / neutral / negative | 2.9K |
| `financial-sentiment-v1.1-base` | valence | same | 4.5K |
| `forward-looking-v1.2-base` | tense | `forward` / `not forward` (space!) | 2.8K |
| `forward-looking-v1.1-base` | tense | same | 724 |
| `prediction-v1.1-base` | modality | `prediction` / `not-prediction` (hyphen!) | 365 |

### Three mandatory usage requirements (per card)
1. `enable_thinking=False` — fine-tuned to emit exactly one label token.
2. **Exact system prompt verbatim** (e.g. `Classify the financial sentiment as positive, neutral, or negative.`) — present on every training example; it's a task key, not a description.
3. **Constrain output** to the label set via regex/grammar/guided decoding. Recommended serving: SGLang (`python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment-v1.2-base`).

⚠️ Label-string inconsistency across the family (`not forward` vs `not-prediction`) — build decoding grammars per checkpoint. Also: `prediction-v1.1` card points at `NOSIBLE/predictive` (not public); assume it's `NOSIBLE/prediction` renamed.

### Benchmarks & training
- financial-sentiment v1.1: 87.70% English; beats FinBERT's 86% on Financial PhraseBank (held out entirely from training). v1.2: English flat (87.97%) but multilingual 76.69%→83.16% and currency/geo feeds 67.30%→76.17% — 94 languages; multilingual is the whole story.
- Disclosed training config (family spec): lr 2e-5, cosine + 0.03 warmup, batch 64, **2 epochs** (deliberate under-training on noisy committee labels), AdamW fused, bf16, **NEFTune α=5**, weight decay 0.1, max len 2048, loss masked to the single assistant label token (`labels=-100` elsewhere).
- Limitations: finance-only, no aspect/entity binding (event layer's job — guide §8), 2048-token context, per-language variance.

## Datasets (3 repos, ODC-By v1.0, 100,000 rows each)

Released 2025-11-26, v1.0.0. Shared schema: `text`, `label`, `netloc`, `url`; single `train` split; English; Parquet. Sourced from **NOSIBLE Search Feeds** on finance queries — already cleaned (smol-html), deduplicated (event layer), on-topic chunks (128–1024-token `n_contextify` window), *not* a random web sample.

| Dataset | Labels | Downloads |
|---|---|---|
| `financial-sentiment` | positive / neutral / negative — by **potential financial impact**, not tone | 73 |
| `forward-looking` | forward / not forward | 26 |
| `prediction` | prediction / not-prediction | 23 |

### Shared annotation pipeline (disclosed, = guide §3)
1. Hand-label ~200 samples for prompt tuning.
2. Label 100k rows with **8 LLM annotators** (Grok 4, Gemini 2.5, GPT variants incl. GPT-5, Llama 4, Qwen3).
3. Train **linear ensemble models over 6 embedding models** — cheap consistent probe whose disagreement with the committee is a free active-learning acquisition function.
4. **GPT-5.1 oracle** adjudicates disagreements iteratively.
5. **Drop** underperforming annotators (pruned, not down-weighted); repeat to convergence.

Consequences: labels are model-derived consensus (shared blind spots included); no published class balance, agreement stats, or eval split — the external PhraseBank benchmark carries the evidential weight.

## The orthogonal-axes design

| Axis | Question | Model |
|---|---|---|
| Valence | Good or bad financial impact? | financial-sentiment |
| Tense | About the future? | forward-looking |
| Modality | Forecast, or report? | prediction |

"We will open 40 stores next year" = forward but **not** a prediction (commitment); "In hindsight, we had forecast a downturn" = not forward but **is** a prediction. Crossing the three separates guidance-from-results and issuer-intent from third-party estimates. The missing axis — *which entity* — is deliberately absent; entity binding happens in the event layer.

## For cybernaut_mini

- Repo mapping: committee → `providers/judge.py`; linear probe → `providers/embeddings.py`; disagreement/oracle loop → `evals.py`; corpus loading → `datasets.py`; distil target → `models.py`.
- **Split by `netloc`, not by row** — random splits leak syndicated wire copy.
- Start the distil loop on `forward-looking` (binary, cleaner agreement stats), then port to 3-class sentiment. `prediction` is the stalest head (no v1.2, name mismatch, fewest downloads) — use compositionally, not as a target.
- **ODC-By attribution required** for any public use: Matthew Dicks, Simon van Dyk, Stuart Reid; NOSIBLE Inc.

305:- **Bloom Filter Reranker -** Each shard has a [bloom filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom_filter) that keeps track of important phrases it contains. If a selected shard hasn't seen any of the user's search intents, then that shard should get downranked.
306:- **Compression Reranker -** Each shard has a trained [Zstandard text compression](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v163/kasturi22a) dictionary. The shard that can compress the input question the best is more likely to contain the most similar content.
307:- **Neural Reranker -** We can also feed the LLM-generated titles and descriptions of each selected shard along with the question into a neural reranker like [bge-reranker-v2-m3](https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3) to get a reranked set of shards.
308:- **Page (Re)Ranker -** Last, but certainly not least, it is also possible to use a nearest neighbor graph and the [Personalized PageRank](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/plofgren/Fast-PPR_KDD_Talk.pdf) algorithm to produce a probability mass over your selected shards.
310:Once again, these ranking factors are then combined using reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). We have also used LLMs to rerank selected shards. That works very well but the added latency is simply too high for a search engine.
314:In the case of the Japanese shards the one and only shard we have that talks about gene editing in Japanese bubbles to the top. In the case of the English shards the shard that actually talks about bacteria and yeast in the context of gene editing bubbles up to the third position. Which is what we want to see.
316:Q: "What lessons from bacteria and yeast actually translate into safer gene-editing medicines?" is routed to these English shards:
326:Q: "細菌と酵母から得られる教訓は、より安全な遺伝子編集医薬品にどのように応用されるのでしょうか？" is routed to these Japanese shards:
336:The translation of shard 200,739 in English is *"Analysis of Pharmaceutical Companies’ Therapeutic Approval, Market Deployment, and Infectious Disease Vaccine Technology Trends in Drug Development and Clinical Trials".*
343:### **7 // Shard-based Question Expansion**
345:Next, we use the synonym graphs in each shard to probabilistically expand our search terms. Because each shard is lexically and semantically coherent, the synonyms in each shard are unambiguous. Put simply, "gene" in shard 11,343 only has the genetic meaning. We don't need to worry that Gene is also a name and, in some other shards, would co-occur a lot with "Willy Wonka".
403:At this point we finally have (1) our instruction-optimized embeddings, (2) our expanded set of search terms, (3) our search intents, and (4) a list of 10-30 shards that almost certainly contain documents that relate directly to our question. This package of information is then broadcast to each of the final shards.

content.text:
Good question, and the answer reframes the corpus problem.

## NOSIBLE's HuggingFace has no retrieval corpus

Confirmed live — the org is 8 repos, unchanged since Dec 2025: 5 Qwen3-0.6B classifiers and **3 datasets** (`financial-sentiment`, `forward-looking`, `prediction`). Those are 100k rows each, schema `text / label / netloc / url`, English, ODC-By. They're **classification training data**, not a searchable corpus — no queries, no qrels, no document IDs. They serve guide §3 (the classifier heads), not the 8-stage retrieval pipeline.

They're still valuable, and uniquely so: the text is drawn from NOSIBLE's own Search Feeds, already smol-html-cleaned and chunked to their 128–1024-token window. That's the only publicly available sample of their actual document distribution. Just not a corpus you can search.

## The real constraint: shards

The blog's architecture is a federation of 250,000 shards, and stages 5–7 — shard selection, shard reranking, shard-based question expansion — exist *only* because the shards do. NOSIBLE calls shard selection "arguably the single most important stage." With SciFact's 5,183 documents you get roughly one shard, which means the three stages the blog cares most about can't be exercised at all. **That's the fidelity argument for scale**, and it's much stronger than a bragging-rights argument.

One thing to flag: the blog's own numbers don't reconcile. "Almost a billion webpages" across 250,000 shards is ~4,000 docs/shard, but the worked example (shard 11,343) reports 134,523 documents — a 34× gap. Either the shard count is aspirational, or "documents" are chunks rather than pages. We'd have to pick an assumption and document it, which is exactly what the repo's Assumptions docstring header is for.

Either way, to make shard *selection* a real decision you want ≥200 shards, so the target is roughly **1M–30M documents** depending on which shard-size reading we adopt.

## Candidates

| Corpus | Scale | Langs | Qrels | Licence | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FineWeb** (`sample-10BT`) | ~10B tokens | en | ✗ | ODC-By | Cleaned CommonCrawl — closest to NOSIBLE's actual input |
| **FineWeb-2** | 1B–10B docs, 1000+ langs | multi | ✗ | ODC-By | Same, plus the Japanese the blog's example needs |
| **MIRACL corpus** | 10M–100M passages, 16 langs | multi | ✓ expert | Apache-2.0 | Only multilingual retrieval eval at this scale |
| **MS MARCO** | 1M–10M | en | ✓ | MS research-only | Classic IR eval; licence restricts use |
| BEIR SciFact | 5,183 | en | ✓ | CC BY-SA | Current choice — ~1 shard, can't test stages 5–7 |
| NOSIBLE ×3 | 300k rows | en | ✗ | ODC-By | Classifier heads only |

My recommendation is a **spine + eval split**: FineWeb-2 as the bulk corpus (gives you real shard structure, is ODC-By, and is cleaned-CommonCrawl like NOSIBLE's own input), with MIRACL folded in as the evaluation substrate — it carries real expert qrels *and* Japanese, so the blog's exact bilingual gene-editing example becomes runnable end to end. NOSIBLE's three datasets then get used for what they actually are: the classifier layer.

**Before the machine question bites:** this container has **7.7 GiB RAM and 8 cores** (355G disk is fine). That caps you around 1–2M documents with int8-quantised embeddings. "Single big machine" needs to mean something bigger than what I'm running in — what are the specs of the box you're targeting, and is it this Mac or something else?

Cross-check is in, and it corrects my scale estimate materially.

**Confirmed, and stronger than I put it:** NOSIBLE's copyright page states outright — *"NOSIBLE is a search and retrieval product, not a bulk web corpus for redistribution."* They also describe open-sourcing *models*, not corpora. **Corrected — the shard ratio.** A primary source I hadn't seen, [Can Faceted Search at Web-Scale Self Organize?](https://nosible.com/research/can-faceted-search-at-web-scale-self-organize), states: *"Our last run learned 250,000 collections from 250,000,000 documents."* That's **1,000 documents per collection** — a far better anchor than anything in the Cybernaut blog. My earlier "1M–30M documents to reach ≥200 shards" was too pessimistic:

| Shards | Docs @ 1,000/shard | Feasible here? |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | 200,000 | Yes, comfortably |
| 1,000 | 1,000,000 | Yes, with int8 |
| 250,000 (full) | 250,000,000 | No |

**A few hundred thousand documents is enough to make shard selection a real decision.** That fits the current 7.7 GiB container, so the machine question stops being a blocker for starting.

The 134,523-document figure for shard 11,343 is still the outlier — 134× the training ratio, and inconsistent with ~1B pages ÷ 250k shards ≈ 4,000. Design toward 1,000–4,000; treat 134k as unexplained rather than resolved.

- **Aho-Corasick is confirmed in production** for per-collection entity tagging — that NOT-BUILT item is real, not inferred
- **Collections are flushed to disk on write and cached in RAM by size/importance** — that is precisely the single-machine architecture we need, straight from the source
- Ingest runs 15–20M pages/day → 91M paragraphs, i.e. **~6 chunks per page** for sizing math
- The ranker is `hybrid-3`; exposed algorithms are `lexical, baseline, hamming, hybrid-1/2/3, company` — a concrete list for `query/` to mirror, and `hamming` corroborates their LSH heritage

**One thing I could not verify:** the 2025-08-26 Cybernaut-1 post promised *"next week, we will be open-sourcing a comprehensive set of evaluations."* I found no such release — not on the NosibleAI GitHub, not elsewhere. Absence of evidence rather than proof, but it means there's no NOSIBLE-published qrels to lean on, so the dual-track eval decision you made stands unchanged.

Two things verified that make this concrete. (I read only the schema section of that 6,442-line FineWeb-2 config dump, not the full per-language listing — the field list is what mattered.)

**FineWeb-2 carries `url`, `date`, `language`, `language_score`, `minhash_cluster_size`.** So it can be filtered by domain and ordered in time.

**And the NOSIBLE preview is more revealing than the card suggests.** Their `netloc` values: `zacks.com`, `fool.com`, `benzinga.com`, `investing.com`, `tradingview.com`, `simplywall.st`, `stocktitan.net`, `rttnews.com`, `hl.co.uk`, `menafn.com`, `ogj.com`, `offshore-mag.com`, `worldconstructionnetwork.com`. That's financial news, trade press, stock-analysis sites and press-release wires — **not a random web sample**.

That reframes your question. NOSIBLE's shards are coherent partly *because their corpus is query-curated news*, not because their clustering is magic. If we cluster raw FineWeb-2 — a broad web sample — our shards will be mushier, and we'd wrongly blame the algorithm. **Corpus composition is a shard-quality lever, not just a scale knob.**

Since both datasets expose the needed columns, there's a move available: extract the `netloc` distribution across all 300k NOSIBLE rows and filter FineWeb-2's `url` to match. That reproduces their corpus *composition* from the only public trace of it. Caveat — those 300k rows were sampled with *finance* queries, so they show the finance slice of their feeds, not the whole index. Their own worked example is gene editing. Domain-matching alone would overfit to finance; it's a seed, not the whole recipe.

## Where quality actually comes from

Shard quality decomposes, and different sources fix different parts:

| Dimension | What breaks without it | Best source |
|---|---|---|
| **Entity index** (stage 5 entity selector, Aho-Corasick tagger) | Entity similarity is a stub | **Wikidata** — CC0, millions of entities, multilingual aliases |
| **Synonym graph** (stage 7 expansion) | Expansion is guesswork | **Wikipedia redirects** — human-curated aliases, free |
| **Cluster coherence** | Mushy shards; stages 5–7 look broken | **CC-News** or netloc-matched FineWeb-2 |
| **Real queries** (stages 1–4, shard `Queries` field) | Every query is synthetic | **ORCAS** — 10M real Bing query→doc pairs |
| **Company entities** (finance vertical) | No ticker/issuer binding | **GLEIF LEI** + **SEC EDGAR** tickers, both open |
| **The blog's own example** | Gene-editing query has no documents | **S2ORC / PubMed** |
| **Event layer / point-in-time** | No temporal network | **GDELT** — free, dated, 15-min updates |

My ranking by leverage per unit of effort: **Wikidata first** — it converts the entity selector from a stub into a real ranking factor, it's CC0, and it feeds the Aho-Corasick tagger we now know is real in production. **Wikipedia second** — redirects give you a synonym graph for free, articles give clean multilingual clusters, and it's the open stand-in for the Wikipedia/LinkedIn/Market-API Resolver they describe. **ORCAS third**, because it partly dissolves the tension you resolved earlier: real queries mean the generated-eval track carries less weight.

Found the pieces, and they point to amending the spine decision.

**CC-News is the realistic answer.** Available and current:

| Dataset | Coverage | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `stanford-oval/ccnews` | 2016 → Jun 2024, 100+ languages | Cleaned, deduplicated, language-tagged |
| `AbedGarra/ccnews2024plus` | Jun 2024 → Jul 2026 | Same pipeline, extends to now |
| `hotchpotch/multilingual_cc_news` | 100M–1B rows, per-language subsets | Updated Jun 2026 |
| `brian-learns/cdx-cc-news` | URL index, MIT | **Query which domains exist before downloading** |

That last one is the unlock for your netloc idea — a CDXj index means we can find NOSIBLE's specific domains inside CC-News without pulling the whole corpus first.

This is a closer match to NOSIBLE on every axis that matters: news-shaped rather than general web, dated (their point-in-time network), 100+ languages across 150+ countries, and continuously extended the way a crawl is. FineWeb-2 would drop from spine to filler — useful where CC-News is thin in a language, and for non-news reference text.

**The honest cost: licensing gets murkier.** FineWeb-2 is cleanly ODC-By. The CC-News derivatives are mostly `license:unknown` (`Geralt-Targaryen/CC-News` is Apache-2.0 but English-only, 2016–2021). NOSIBLE themselves rely on search-engine fair-use doctrine for their crawl rather than a data licence — which is coherent for them and less so for a repo that publishes artifacts. Your locked decision 3 was emphatic about attribution and licence files, so this genuinely cuts against it.

One more consequence worth naming: MIRACL is Wikipedia-derived, so its qrels won't judge a news corpus. It stays as a **separately indexed benchmark collection** — which is exactly what your "clearly separated namespaces" decision already implies, so nothing breaks, but the real-qrels track will be measuring a different corpus than the one shards are learned over.

"""Embedding providers behind a common protocol.

Three providers, in ascending order of cost:

``Model2VecEmbedder`` is the DEFAULT. Static (lookup-table) embeddings distilled
from a real transformer — semantic structure without torch, so it ships in the
core dependencies rather than an extra. It is what shard learning needs: shards
are k-means clusters over document vectors, and clustering only produces coherent
shards if the vector space carries meaning.

``HashEmbedder`` is a deterministic offline provider (feature hashing of tokens and
character trigrams), not a test mock. It is real, fast and needs no download, but
feature hashing has NO semantic structure — documents about the same topic land in
unrelated buckets. It is therefore correct for offline/deterministic tests and
WRONG for learning shards. It is no longer the default for exactly that reason.

``SentenceTransformersEmbedder`` wraps E5-style models and is the quality ceiling;
it needs the optional 'st' extra (torch) and downloads weights on first use.

Blog reference: "The Road to Cybernaut-1", stage 5 (Shard Selection) — the dense
selector compares question embeddings against shard summary embeddings, so shard
quality is bounded above by embedding quality.

Assumptions: model2vec's distilled vectors are close enough to their teacher to
cluster comparably. Not verified here; the ablation belongs in evals.
Alternatives rejected: keeping the hash embedder as default (cheap, but yields
incoherent shards and would make stages 5-7 look broken when the fault is the
embedder); making sentence-transformers the default (best vectors, but pulls torch
into every install and breaks a bare `kedro run`).
"""

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")

    # works on the default install. 'sentence_transformers' is the quality option but
    # lives behind the optional 'st' extra, so it must be opted into explicitly
    # (configs/default.yaml, or --env prod).
    provider: Literal["hash", "sentence_transformers"] = "hash"
    model: str = "intfloat/multilingual-e5-small"
    revision: str | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description=(
            "Commit SHA or tag of the model weights. None resolves to the repo's "
            "default branch and is not reproducible; pin it for production builds."
        ),
    )
    dim: int = Field(default=256, ge=8, description="Vector size for the hash provider")

    def is_pinned(self) -> bool:
        """True when this configuration identifies exactly one set of weights."""
        if self.provider == "hash":
            # The hash embedder is pure code — no weights to drift.
            return True
        revision = self.revision
        if revision is None:
            return False
        return revision.strip().lower() not in {"main", "master", "head"}
